children: Tata Trusts Chairman Noel N Tata has flagged concerns over the proposed public listing of the Tata Group, warning that such a move could fundamentally alter the group's philosophy, with profits potentially taking precedence over philanthropy as its shareholder base expands.

Speaking at the HT Leadership Summit 2026, Noel said a public listing could change the way the Tata Group operates. He added that Tata Trusts would work constructively with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group's founding ethos.

My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working,TATA TRUSTS CHAIRMAN NOEL N TATA
He added that the continuity of the Tata way remained important, emphasising that the group's philosophy should remain independent of individual leadership and personalities.
"Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he said.
Tata Group's direction is right, but execution needs greater discipline

Noel said the group's strategic direction, particularly its focus on philanthropy and nation-building, remained unchanged. However, he stressed the need for greater discipline in executing large projects, especially those with long gestation periods.
"I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," he said.
He pointed to project execution and capital allocation as key areas requiring attention, arguing that even well-conceived projects could struggle without the necessary discipline.
"The direction is fine, but we also need discipline in the execution of these very large projects," Noel added.
Westside eyes 500-plus stores as consumption grows across India

On the retail business, Noel said Westside currently operates around 320 stores and is looking to expand its network to more than 500 outlets, citing the sharp rise in consumption across India's socio-economic categories over the past decade.
He credited the country's consumption growth for creating opportunities for organised retail, saying demand was expanding across markets without a clear divide between consumer segments.

"In the last ten years, consumption has just skyrocketed in India across different socio-economic categories to the point that today we are 320-odd stores and we are looking to see when we can reach 500-plus stores of Westside," he said.

Noel also spoke about Westside's early strategy of adopting a private-label model, which involved controlling the product journey from fabric and design to the final customer. He described the approach as making Tata an early direct-to-consumer (D2C) player in India.
Zudio targets bottom of the pyramid with aspirational fashion
Explaining the thinking behind Zudio's launch in 2016, Noel said the brand was created to cater to consumers at the bottom of the pyramid by offering aspirational products at affordable prices.

He said the company recognised that the desire for better products was not restricted to affluent consumers or metropolitan cities, prompting it to build a retail format around accessibility and affordability.

Zudio initially offered products at starting price points of ₹199, with prices going up to ₹999, and was designed as an air-conditioned, approximately 6,000-square-foot store. Noel said the starting price points had remained unchanged over the past decade.
Tata sees itself as a partner in India's development
Noel also spoke about the group's contribution to India's industrial development, pointing to its investments in emerging sectors such as semiconductors and electric vehicle (EV) batteries.

He said the Tata Group viewed itself as a partner in India's development, with its investments extending beyond conventional businesses into areas that could support the country's long-term industrial ambitions.
Taking over Tata Trusts gave Noel a deeper understanding of India's underserved

Reflecting on his experience as Chairman of Tata Trusts, Noel said taking on the role gave him a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by underserved communities and the opportunity for philanthropy to make a difference.
He said the scale of the problems faced by sections of society had given him a sense of humility, while also highlighting the significant scope for the Trusts to contribute towards addressing them.

title: Listing could change the Tata way: Noel Tata flags concerns over profits taking precedence over philanthropy
